question: Why do trees cool streets?

sources.title: How trees cool a city: shade and evapotranspiration
How much can trees cool a city? Global review of 182 studies (Li et al. 2024)
Why 40% tree canopy matters: block-scale cooling (Ziter et al. 2019)
What is an urban heat island? Why pavement and buildings make cities hotter

text: Trees cool streets in two ways. First, their crowns block sunlight before it reaches the ground, so shaded pavement and walls stay cooler [1]. Second, trees pull water up through their roots and release it as vapor from their leaves; turning water into vapor uses heat, which cools the surrounding air [1]. A global review of 182 studies found that urban trees can lower street-level temperatures by as much as 12°C, depending on the climate, the shape of the city and the kinds of trees [2]. Block-scale cooling is strongest once canopy reaches about 40% [3].

question: Why is my neighborhood hotter?

sources.title: Are redlined neighborhoods hotter? (Hoffman, Shandas & Pendleton 2020)
Do lower-income neighborhoods have fewer trees and more heat? (McDonald et al. 2021)
What is an urban heat island? Why pavement and buildings make cities hotter
Code Red: Baltimore's hottest neighborhoods, like McElderry Park, are poorer and have fewer trees

text: Your neighborhood might be hotter because it has fewer trees and more pavement, which traps heat. Studies show that low-income areas often have significantly less tree cover and are 1.5°C (2.7°F) warmer than higher-income ones [2]. Additionally, dense rows of buildings can create "urban canyons" that block breezes and trap hot air inside [3]. This creates a heat island effect where the ground and roofs absorb more sun energy than natural areas do [3].

question: Which tree fits a narrow sidewalk?

sources.title: Small street trees for Baltimore (under 35 ft, OK under power lines): eastern redbud, serviceberry, and why hedge maple is no longer allowed
How big does a street tree pit need to be in Baltimore? Minimum tree pit size and soil volume

text: For a narrow sidewalk, look at small trees. Baltimore's approved list puts eastern redbud and Canadian serviceberry in its small group: trees under 35 feet at maturity that suit narrow streets, small tree pits and spots under overhead wires. Both are native [1]. Avoid hedge maple: the city now lists it as invasive and not to be planted [1]. Every street tree pit must be at least 48 square feet, with at least 144 cubic feet of soil [2]. Before planting in the public right-of-way, you need permission from the city's Forestry Division [1].

question: How can I help?

sources.title: How do I request a street tree for my street in Baltimore?
Volunteer with Baltimore Tree Trust (tree planting nonprofit)
TreeKeepers: free tree planting and pruning training in Baltimore
How to donate to Baltimore tree planting groups

text: There are several ways to help. Ask the city to plant a street tree in front of your home with TreeBaltimore's Street Tree Request form [1]. Volunteer at Baltimore Tree Trust's spring and fall plantings; no experience is needed [2]. Take TreeBaltimore's free TreeKeepers training to learn to plant and care for trees [3]. Or donate to local tree groups such as TreeBaltimore, Baltimore Tree Trust, Blue Water Baltimore or Parks & People [4].
